sentences.text: The defining feature of the holotype is a set of three posterior dorsal vertebrae catalogued as NHMUK PV R 1828.
Friedrich von Huene established the genus in 1923 based on these vertebrae, which possess very high spines that inspired the Latin name meaning 'high with spines'.
The type species designated for this genus is Altispinax dunkeri.
Gregory Paul once estimated that this predator weighed one tonne and was shorter than the eight-meter-long type specimen of Acrocanthosaurus atokensis.
Ralph Molnar suggested that the two vertebrae nearest the skull were fused, interpreting the front spines as evidence of a healed injury to a back frill.
Fossil collector Samuel Husbands Beckles found nodules containing dinosaur bones near Battle, East Sussex, likely in the early 1850s, and Richard Owen reported these finds in 1856.
The species name honors paleontologist Wilhelm Dunker, who discovered a tooth in Deister years prior, and the holotype was added to the University of Marburg collection under catalog number UM 84.
Darren Naish proposed in 2003 that the gap between the front spines was natural rather than the result of injury.

The classification of Altispinax is debated, with placements ranging from Eustreptospondylidae to Allosauroidea, though most researchers currently place it in Tetanurae incertae sedis within the class Reptilia and parent group Theropoda.
It is debated whether Altispinax is valid, as later research suggested the type specimen, a tooth, was not diagnostic, making it a nomen dubium with no probable connection to the spines.

George Olshevsky named the genus Becklespinax in 1991 for the Altispinax vertebrae to honor the original discoverer, Samuel Husbands Beckles, while four additional species were named within the genus before being reclassified, including Altispinax oweni transferred to Valdoraptor and Altispinax parkeri renamed Metriacanthosaurus, a name now considered a modern synonym of Becklespinax.
Altispinax was a large predatory theropod dinosaur that lived between 140 and 133 million years ago in what is now East Sussex, England, during the early Cretaceous period in the Valanginian stage.
